query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy nanoalloy films maintain structural and chemical stability at high temperatures because a synergy between short-range ordering and constrained grain-boundary mobility effectively suppresses grain coarsening and interfacial chemical segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nano-grained high-entropy alloy films with a controlled, uniform grain-size distribution and defined grain-boundary character (e.g., controlled fractions of high-angle and low-angle boundaries)
generation.intervention: Expose films with tailored boundary configurations to elevated temperatures (up to ~1200 K) under inert or vacuum conditions while monitoring their evolution via in situ high-temperature TEM and synchrotron diffraction.
generation.conditions: Under high-temperature conditions (up to the alloy's solid-solution limit, ~1200 K) in environments that minimize oxidation, comparing films engineered for boundary character versus films with standard, uniform boundaries
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary structure, specifically the nature and density of interfaces that support short-range ordering
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, films with boundary characters that promote short-range ordering exhibit slowed atomic diffusion across grain boundaries. This limited mobility reduces grain growth and prevents the onset of deleterious chemical segregation, thereby preserving the alloy’s overall structural and chemical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Films engineered to have a higher fraction of grain boundaries conducive to short-range order will display reduced grain coarsening, minimal interfacial segregation, and sustained stability relative to films with standard boundary distributions.
generation.baseline: Films with a uniform grain-size distribution and naturally occurring grain-boundary characteristics processed by conventional methods
generation.boundary: The prediction applies for high-temperature exposure up to around 1200 K under inert or vacuum conditions; deviations may occur if environmental oxidation or phase transformations beyond the solid-solution range are present.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of short-range ordering versus the reduction in grain-boundary mobility are not fully determined, leaving uncertainty as to their relative impact on overall stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy films: one set with engineered boundaries (with a higher proportion of boundaries expected to promote short-range ordering) and a control set with conventional, uniform boundary characteristics. Subject both sets to in situ high-temperature TEM and synchrotron diffraction analysis while heating in an inert or vacuum environment up to ~1200 K over identical time intervals.
measurements: Grain size distribution before and after heat treatment
Chemical homogeneity and interfacial segregation via elemental mapping (e.g., EDS)
Intensity and prevalence of short-range ordering signatures in diffraction patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both engineered and control films exhibit similar grain growth, comparable levels of interfacial segregation, and no significant differences in short-range order during or after high-temperature exposure, then the hypothesis that a synergy between short-range ordering and reduced grain-boundary mobility governs stability is falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . A key component in current tokamak designs is the divertor, which will be in contact with the deuterium-tritium (D-T) plasma and sustain severe fluxes of particles (helium (He) ash, D and T) and heat, along with radiation damage induced by high-energy neutrons [2] , [3] . Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] . Various industrial and advanced functional applications require materials with high strength and ductility. Unfortunately, conventional processing strategies usually attain high material strength at the expense of deteriorated ductility [1] – [3] , whilst developing structures with substantial improvement of both strength and ductility is highly challenging. Recent successes in synthesizing superhard materials [4] – [6] have made the high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment [7] , [8] promising to achieve extreme properties in materials. The combination of pressure and temperature offers the great prospect for altering the microstructure of structural materials that would permit overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off. Given the vast space of control parameters involved in the HPHT treatment and the often complex microstructural evolution under extreme pressures and temperatures [9] , [10] , it remains difficult to predict and interpret the mechanical behaviors of HPHT-treated structural materials, especially the abnormal kinetics and thermodynamics of non-equilibrium interfaces induced by the HPHT treatment [11] , [12] .

decision.trend: Recent studies of high-entropy nano-structured refractory alloys have shown encouraging thermal stability but have not conclusively identified the underlying stabilizing factors. In 2020 (PMC7304825), a nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV film exhibited improved hardness and wear resistance up to 300 °C after post-deposition annealing, suggesting that nano-scale structures in HEAs can be robust under moderate heat. In 2023 (PMC10154406), a sputtered quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf alloy film with an initial average grain size of ~25 nm retained exceptional structural stability, minimal grain growth, and enhanced hardness under irradiation at ~900 °C (1173 K). Yet, questions remain about the precise interplay of interface structures, short-range ordering, and sluggish diffusion in granting both chemical homogeneity and structural integrity at high temperatures in these nanoalloys.
decision.unsolved: Although these film-scale tests suggest that nano-grained high-entropy alloys can be remarkably stable at elevated temperature, the exact mechanism behind their simultaneous structural and chemical stability remains uncertain. It is unclear whether the key factor is short-range ordering, slowed boundary or lattice diffusion, or a more complex interplay of these effects at the nano-scale. A controlled, mechanistic understanding is needed to determine how these features evolve under high-temperature conditions and to distinguish among competing explanations for the origin of the stability in high-entropy nanoalloys.
decision.lever: Conduct an in situ high-temperature TEM and synchrotron diffraction study to track structural evolution of nano-grained films with varied initial interface densities, paired with atomistic or phase-field simulations of grain growth and segregation in the same alloys. Key parameters will include the initial grain-size distribution (particularly controlling the fraction of high-angle vs. low-angle boundaries) and thermal exposure range up to ~1200 K. The hypothesis to test is that a synergy of short-range ordering and constrained grain-boundary mobility under high entropy conditions drives the observed stability. The controlled comparison is between films prepared with different boundary configurations, where the baseline has a relatively uniform grain-size distribution. If the hypothesized synergy is correct, adaptation of boundary character with temperature will be correlated with reduced coarsening, a low density of chemical inhomogeneities, and minimal interfacial segregation. This prediction holds for temperatures up to near the alloy’s solid-solution range under vacuum or inert environments conducive to minimal oxidation. Evidence from prior studies (PMC7304825, PMC10154406) shows improved high-temperature and irradiation stability in nano-structured high-entropy films, supporting the proposed approach. A falsifying outcome would be that films with systematically different boundary structures show similar degradation, implying that short-range ordering and boundary-engineering are not the main causes of thermochemical stability.
decision.why: These experiments and simulations directly address the question of how high-entropy nanoalloys retain structural and chemical stability at high temperature without adding new elements. The approach isolates boundary-related mechanisms and short-range ordering effects, providing a clear test of the proposed mechanistic hypothesis that slowed diffusion at interfaces, together with compositional homogeneity imparted by high entropy, underpins the remarkable stability. By comparing in situ observations with modeling, it will be possible to discern whether grain-boundary dynamics or local ordering is the key lever controlling stability, thereby advancing fundamental understanding and guiding robust alloy design.
